title: CodeQuest
tagline: Making technical interview prep less lonely

metadata.label: GOAL
metadata.value: Bring interview practice and peer connection into one experience.

introParagraphs: Technical interview prep usually happens alone. Networking is something students know they should do, but often don't know how to start.
CodeQuest brings both together through peer-to-peer technical interview sessions where students alternate between solving problems and reviewing each other.
description: Peer-to-peer technical interview practice platform where students alternate between solving problems and reviewing each other.

heroMedia.caption: CodeQuest brings interview practice and peer connection into one experience through peer-to-peer sessions.

caseStudy.heading: Students were preparing for careers across disconnected tools.
body: We interviewed six CS students about how they prepared for jobs, approached networking, and used career-prep tools.

cards.title: Interview prep happened alone
cards.body: Students were teaching themselves through tools like LeetCode and YouTube.

cards.title: Networking felt awkward to start
cards.body: Students understood its importance, but many wished they had started sooner and didn't know how.

cards.title: Everything lived somewhere different
cards.body: Practice, networking, and events happened across separate platforms rather than one connected experience.

caseStudy.largeQuestion: How might we make technical interview practice social enough that students build connections while preparing for jobs?
caseStudy.conclusion: This HMW is a synthesis for the case study—not wording from the original research.

caseStudy.placeholderTitle: LeetCode [Practice] ↘  YouTube [Learning] → CS STUDENT ← Networking [Connections] ↗ Events [Opportunities]
caseStudy.caption: Career prep fragmentation: students navigated independent study, passive learning, and cold networking across isolated tools.

caseStudy.heading: Instead of building another solo practice tool, we made students useful to each other.
body: Our concept centered around one interaction:

cards.title: CHALLENGER
cards.body: Solve a live coding problem while explaining your thinking.

cards.title: REVIEWER
cards.body: Observe the solution, follow the challenger's reasoning, and provide structured feedback.

caseStudy.conclusion: The challenger practices technical and communication skills while the reviewer gets exposure to another person's problem-solving approach. Both students meet another peer in the process.

caseStudy.placeholderTitle: CHALLENGER [Solve ↓ Explain]  ↔  LIVE SESSION  ↔  [Observe ↓ Review] REVIEWER
caseStudy.caption: Practice technical skills · Practice communication · Learn by reviewing · Meet another CS student

caseStudy.heading: Turning networking into a side effect
caseStudy.subheading: We designed the session around doing something together—not introducing yourself.
context: Our interviews suggested students understood networking mattered, but initiating it felt awkward.
That made us question whether CodeQuest should explicitly feel like a networking platform.
decision: Instead, we centered the experience around a shared task.
Two students aren't matched just to: “Network.”
They're matched to solve and review a problem together. The connection happens through the activity.
why: This gives both people an immediate reason to interact.
Instead of: Meet stranger → figure out what to say → maybe build connection
CodeQuest becomes: Join session → solve together → exchange feedback → connection forms naturally
caseStudy.caption: Challenger practices explaining their reasoning; Reviewer learns from another approach while providing feedback.

cards.title: Reviewer
cards.body: Learns from another approach while providing feedback.

caseStudy.heading: Giving career prep one starting point
caseStudy.subheading: We brought sessions, practice, and progress into one dashboard.
context: Our research showed students were switching between separate tools for practice, networking, and events.
decision: We designed the dashboard as the starting point for the experience.
Students could see: Upcoming sessions, Session scheduling, Practice challenges, Past sessions, Challenge streaks, Progress.
The goal was to reduce the feeling of career preparation being scattered across unrelated tools. The prototype shown combines those elements into one dashboard.
caseStudy.caption: Centralizing upcoming sessions, practice challenges, history, and streaks into one starting point.

caseStudy.heading: The concept made sense. Some of our interface language didn't.
body: We tested the prototype with two CS students.
Each participant completed both sides of the experience:

cards.title: Task 1 — Challenger
cards.body: Find an active session, join it, complete the challenge, and submit.

cards.title: Task 2 — Reviewer
cards.body: Schedule a reviewer session, join, evaluate the challenger, and submit feedback.

caseStudy.conclusion: Testing revealed several places where our mental model didn't match the users'.

caseStudy.heading: The dashboard looked actionable to us. Users didn't see it that way.
body: What we designed: The dashboard CTA said: VIEW SESSION.
What happened: Both participants navigated toward the sidebar rather than relying on the dashboard button. The wording also failed to communicate that selecting it meant actively joining the session.
Next iteration: VIEW SESSION ↓ JOIN SESSION. And make today's session the strongest action on the dashboard.
caseStudy.placeholderTitle: DASHBOARD CTA: VIEW SESSION → JOIN SESSION
caseStudy.caption: Why it changed: “View” described content consumption. “Join” describes the action the user is actually taking.

caseStudy.heading: We showed users the tool before telling them what to solve.
body: What we designed: When a challenger entered a session, the coding environment was immediately prominent.
What happened: Participants expected to understand the challenge before interacting with the editor.
Next iteration: Make the problem statement the default view. Then offer a split-screen option for users who want the problem and editor visible simultaneously.
caseStudy.beforeLabel: BEFORE: CODE EDITOR (Problem hidden behind tab)
caseStudy.placeholderTitle: CHALLENGER WORKSPACE: TOOL FIRST → PROBLEM FIRST
caseStudy.caption: Before: The interface prioritized the tool. After: The interface prioritized understanding the task.

caseStudy.heading: Solving was rewarding. Reviewing didn't feel equally valuable.
caseStudy.subheading: The second half of our peer system needed more reason to participate.
context: CodeQuest depends on people being willing to play both roles.

Testing revealed that the reviewer experience didn't feel particularly meaningful or rewarding. Participants also struggled to find the solution tab, and the grading controls and instructions were unclear.
decision: We proposed four architectural improvements to elevate the reviewer role:

decisionPoints.title: Clearer evaluation instructions
decisionPoints.body: Explain exactly what reviewers should assess.

decisionPoints.title: Better information architecture
decisionPoints.body: Make the solution easier to find.

caseStudy.caption: Elevating reviewer recognition turns peer evaluation into a rewarding and motivating learning activity.

caseStudy.heading: Prep. Connect. Compete.
body: CodeQuest turns interview prep from an isolated activity into a repeated cycle of practicing, reviewing, and meeting other students.
The original project framing described CodeQuest as “one platform to prep, connect, and compete.”

caseStudy.caption: Product sequence from dashboard match entry to collaborative problem-solving and structured peer feedback.

caseStudy.heading: Testing the two roles changed how I thought about the product.
body: The strongest learning wasn't just about button labels.
It exposed a deeper product challenge: A peer-to-peer system only works if participating feels valuable from both sides.
If I continued CodeQuest, I'd explore three questions:

items.heading: How do we make reviewing as valuable as solving?
items.body: Without enough reviewers, the session model breaks down.

items.heading: How much structure should a mock interview provide?
items.body: Too little guidance creates confusion. Too much could make the experience feel unlike a real interview.

items.heading: Does practicing together actually make networking easier?
items.body: Our research motivated the idea, but we'd need longer-term testing to determine whether repeated sessions actually create meaningful connections.
